proxy_language: Proto-Algonquian-flavored Plains stand-in (speculative), with Proto-Siouan and Proto-Uto-Aztecan as alternates
proxy_rationale: Folsom (c. 12,900-12,000 cal BP, Great Plains) is known only from lithic and bison-kill archaeology; no language can be linked to it. All Plains language families (Siouan, Algonquian, Uto-Aztecan, Kiowa-Tanoan, Caddoan, Athabaskan) arrived or diversified far later, so any proxy is a notational convenience, not a claim of descent. Proto-Algonquian is chosen only because its reconstruction (Bloomfield 1946; Aubin 1975; Siebert) is well documented, has simple CV(C) phonotactics, polysynthetic root+final structure, and gives transparent compound-like noun building. The names should read as Great Plains-sounding hunter vocabulary, not as a real Folsom language.
phonology: Proto-Algonquian (Bloomfield 1946): consonants *p *t *c (affricate, written c) *k *s *S (sh) *x (uncertain, often written *x or *hk cluster) *h *m *n *l *θ (th) *w *y; vowels short *a *e *i *o and long *aa *ee *ii *oo. Distinctive: preaspirated clusters (*hk *ht *hc *hp), *l and *θ later merging in daughters.
phonotactics: Syllable shapes CV, CVC, V; codas occur almost only as the first member of a medial cluster (VC.CV) with h, s, S, x, or a nasal as first member (e.g. *-hk-, *-ht-, *-sk-, *-mp-). No word-initial clusters. Words are typically vowel-final (nouns) or built from root + medial + final. Clusters with *w or *y as second member are rare; geminates absent in reconstruction.
orthography: Reconstruction notation with asterisk (Bloomfield): c for the affricate, S for sh, q (Proto-Algonquian sometimes uses *q), long vowels doubled (aa ee ii oo). For game names written in Latin script, use plain letters p t c k s sh h m n l th w y with a e i o and doubled long vowels; no asterisk in the displayed name.
morphology: Polysynthetic, agglutinating, root + medial + final stem formation. Nouns are animate or inanimate (gender), with suffixes for plural (-ak animate, -ali inanimate), obviative (-ali), locative (-ink), diminutive (-ESa). Possession by person prefixes (ne- 1st, ke- 2nd, we- 3rd). Verbs dominate the lexicon; many nouns are verb-derived (agent nouns, instruments) with finals such as -wa, -ki, -wi.
compounding: Compounds are formed by initial + (medial) + final stem combination; modifier precedes head (e.g. adjectival initial + noun final). Linking vowel -i- or -o- between elements is common (e.g. mahk-i-). Genitive-like phrases are usually done by possessed noun with 3rd-person prefix or by compounding; 'X of Y' is rendered as Y-X (modifier first) or by locative -ink 'at/in'. Agent noun 'maker/hunter of Y' = Y + verb final + agent suffix (-ya / -ht).
noun_phrase_order: Modifier-head (adjective/quantifier before noun); possessor before possessed in compounds. Demonstratives precede noun.
sources: Bloomfield, L. 1946 Algonquian (in Linguistic Structures of Native America)
Goddard, I. 1979 Comparative Algonquian (in The Languages of Native America)
Siebert, F. 1975 Resurrecting Virginia Algonquian from the dead
Hofman, J. L. & Amick, D. S. (eds) Folsom archaeology literature (for the archaeological culture, not language)
notes: No language is attested for the Folsom culture, so this is a purely speculative phonological proxy: names should sound like plausible Plains hunter-gatherer words, not claim to be Folsom speech. Not Diaithiris. No word may be identical to a Modern Irish, Scottish Gaelic or Manx word (language is not Goidelic); the Proto-Algonquian-style phonology makes accidental matches unlikely but they should be checked.
